latest_nl_proof:
Fix integers m\ge 2 and g\ge 0. We prove that the numerical semigroups of multiplicity m and genus g are in bijection with the set K_{m,g}.

We use the standard definitions.
A numerical semigroup is a cofinite submonoid S of \mathbb N_0 containing 0. Its multiplicity is its least positive element, denoted m(S). Its genus is g(S):=|\mathbb N_0\setminus S|. For a nonzero m\in S, the Apéry set of S with respect to m is
Ap(S,m):=\{w\in S: w-m\notin S\}.
It is standard and easy to check that Ap(S,m) contains exactly one element in each residue class mod m; thus we may write
Ap(S,m)=\{w_0,w_1,\dots,w_{m-1}\}
with w_0=0 and w_i\equiv i\pmod m for 1\le i\le m-1.
Since m is the multiplicity, no positive integer <m belongs to S, hence for i=1,\dots,m-1 we have w_i>i. Therefore each w_i has the form
w_i=i+m x_i
with x_i\in \mathbb Z_{>0}.
The tuple x=(x_1,\dots,x_{m-1}) is the Kunz-coordinate vector of S.

We first show that if S has multiplicity m and genus g, then its Kunz-coordinate vector lies in K_{m,g}.

Let S be a numerical semigroup with multiplicity m and genus g. Define x_i by w_i=i+m x_i as above.

1. Positivity.
For each i\in\{1,\dots,m-1\}, we have x_i\ge 1 because w_i>i.

2. Kunz inequalities.
Take any i,j\in\{1,\dots,m-1\}.
Because w_i,w_j\in S and S is closed under addition, w_i+w_j\in S.

If i+j<m, then w_i+w_j\equiv i+j\pmod m. Since w_{i+j} is the least element of S congruent to i+j mod m, we have
w_i+w_j\ge w_{i+j}.
Substituting w_k=k+m x_k gives
(i+m x_i)+(j+m x_j)\ge (i+j)+m x_{i+j},
so m(x_i+x_j)\ge m x_{i+j}, hence
x_i+x_j\ge x_{i+j}.

If i+j>m, then w_i+w_j\equiv i+j-m\pmod m. Again by minimality of the Apéry representative in that residue class,
w_i+w_j\ge w_{i+j-m}.
Substituting,
(i+m x_i)+(j+m x_j)\ge (i+j-m)+m x_{i+j-m}.
Since i+j=(i+j-m)+m, this becomes
m(x_i+x_j+1)\ge m x_{i+j-m},
so
x_i+x_j+1\ge x_{i+j-m}.
Thus all required inequalities hold.

3. Sum equals genus.
For each residue class i\in\{1,\dots,m-1\}, the numbers congruent to i mod m that are smaller than w_i are exactly
i,\ i+m,\ i+2m,\ \dots,\ i+(x_i-1)m,
and there are exactly x_i of them. By definition of w_i as the least element of S in that residue class, all these x_i numbers are gaps of S. Conversely, every gap of S is of this form for a unique residue class i\in\{1,\dots,m-1\}. Therefore
g(S)=\sum_{i=1}^{m-1} x_i.
Since g(S)=g, we get x_1+\cdots+x_{m-1}=g.

So x\in K_{m,g}. This defines a map
\Phi:\{S: S \text{ numerical semigroup with } m(S)=m,\ g(S)=g\}\to K_{m,g},
\Phi(S)=(x_1,\dots,x_{m-1}).

Now we construct the inverse map. Let x=(x_1,\dots,x_{m-1})\in K_{m,g}. Define
w_0:=0,\qquad w_i:=i+m x_i\quad (1\le i\le m-1),
and set
S_x:=\{w_i+qm: 0\le i\le m-1,\ q\in \mathbb N_0\}.
Equivalently, S_x is the set generated by the arithmetic tails starting at the w_i.
We prove that S_x is a numerical semigroup of multiplicity m and genus g.

First, S_x\subseteq \mathbb N_0 contains 0, because w_0=0.
Also m=w_0+m\in S_x.

We next prove closure under addition. Take arbitrary a,b\in S_x. Write
a=w_i+pm,\qquad b=w_j+qm
for some i,j\in\{0,1,\dots,m-1\} and p,q\in\mathbb N_0. Then
a+b=(w_i+w_j)+(p+q)m.
So it is enough to show that w_i+w_j\in S_x for all i,j.

- If i=0 or j=0, then w_i+w_j is just w_j or w_i, hence belongs to S_x.
- If 1\le i,j\le m-1 and i+j<m, then by the defining inequality of K_{m,g}, x_i+x_j\ge x_{i+j}. Therefore
w_i+w_j-w_{i+j}=(i+m x_i)+(j+m x_j)-((i+j)+m x_{i+j})=m(x_i+x_j-x_{i+j})\in m\mathbb N_0.
Hence w_i+w_j=w_{i+j}+tm for some t\in\mathbb N_0, so w_i+w_j\in S_x.
- If 1\le i,j\le m-1 and i+j>m, then x_i+x_j+1\ge x_{i+j-m}. Therefore
w_i+w_j-w_{i+j-m}=(i+m x_i)+(j+m x_j)-((i+j-m)+m x_{i+j-m})
=m(x_i+x_j+1-x_{i+j-m})\in m\mathbb N_0.
So again w_i+w_j\in S_x.
- If i+j=m, then
w_i+w_j=(i+m x_i)+(j+m x_j)=m(1+x_i+x_j)=w_0+(1+x_i+x_j)m\in S_x.
Thus S_x is closed under addition.

Next we show cofinite. For each residue class i mod m, all integers of the form w_i+qm (q\ge 0) belong to S_x, so every sufficiently large integer in each residue class lies in S_x. Hence only finitely many nonnegative integers are missing from S_x, and S_x is a numerical semigroup.

Now determine its multiplicity. We already know m\in S_x. For 1\le i\le m-1, positivity of x_i gives w_i=i+m x_i\ge i+m>m. Thus no element of S_x in a nonzero residue class is less than or equal to m. Also in residue class 0 the positive elements are positive multiples of m, so the smallest positive one is m. Therefore the multiplicity of S_x is exactly m.

Now determine its genus. In residue class i\in\{1,\dots,m-1\}, the least element of S_x is w_i=i+m x_i. Hence the missing nonnegative integers in that residue class are exactly
i,\ i+m,\dots, i+(x_i-1)m,
so there are exactly x_i of them. In residue class 0 there are no gaps, since 0,m,2m,\dots all lie in S_x. Therefore
g(S_x)=\sum_{i=1}^{m-1} x_i=g.

Thus x determines a numerical semigroup S_x of multiplicity m and genus g. This gives a map
\Psi:K_{m,g}\to \{S: S \text{ numerical semigroup with } m(S)=m,\ g(S)=g\}.

Finally we check that \Phi and \Psi are inverse to each other.

- Start from a semigroup S. Its Apéry representatives are w_i=i+m x_i by definition of \Phi. The construction of \Psi from x produces exactly the set of all numbers w_i+qm with q\ge 0. But every element s\in S has a unique residue class i mod m; subtracting suitable multiples of m (which belong to S because m\in S) shows that s can be written as w_i+qm with q\ge 0, while every such number lies in S because w_i,m\in S. Hence \Psi(\Phi(S))=S.
- Start from x\in K_{m,g}. In S_x, for each i\in\{1,\dots,m-1\}, the least element congruent to i mod m is exactly w_i=i+m x_i, since all smaller numbers in that residue class are the listed x_i gaps. Therefore the Kunz coordinate recovered by \Phi from S_x is exactly x. So \Phi(\Psi(x))=x.

Therefore \Phi is a bijection between the set of numerical semigroups with multiplicity m and genus g and the set K_{m,g}. Consequently their cardinalities are equal:
N(m,g)=|K_{m,g}|.
This is exactly the claimed statement.
role_in_parent: Translates the original theorem into a cardinality inequality for the combinatorial sets K_{m,g}.
statement_nl: Let m be an integer with m >= 2 and let g be an integer with g >= 0. Define K_{m,g} to be the set of all tuples x = (x_1,...,x_{m-1}) of positive integers such that x satisfies the Kunz inequalities for multiplicity m, namely: for all i,j in {1,...,m-1}, if i + j < m then x_i + x_j >= x_{i+j}, and if i + j > m then x_i + x_j + 1 >= x_{i+j-m}, and such that x_1 + ... + x_{m-1} = g. Then N(m,g), the number of numerical semigroups of multiplicity m and genus g, is equal to the cardinality of K_{m,g}.

domain_restrictions: x = (x_1,...,x_{m-1}) with each x_k ∈ Z_{>0} (positive integers)
case split conditions: if i+j < m then inequality involves x_{i+j}; if i+j > m then inequality involves x_{i+j-m} (which is within {1,...,m-1})
statement_semantic_sketch.normalized_claim: Fix integers m>=2 and g>=0. Let K_{m,g} be the set of tuples x=(x_1,...,x_{m-1}) with x_k>0 for all k and x_1+...+x_{m-1}=g, such that for every i,j∈{1,...,m-1}: (i+j<m ⇒ x_i+x_j≥x_{i+j}) and (i+j>m ⇒ x_i+x_j+1≥x_{i+j-m}). Then the number N(m,g) of numerical semigroups with multiplicity m and genus g equals the cardinality |K_{m,g}|.
quantifier_order: For all integers m with m >= 2
For all integers g with g >= 0
K_{m,g} = { x : (x is a tuple (x_1,...,x_{m-1})) such that (x_1+...+x_{m-1}=g) and (for all i,j in {1,...,m-1}, the Kunz inequalities hold under the stated cases) }

witness_dependencies: Any inequalities are universal over i,j; no existential witnesses are introduced beyond choosing x as an element of K_{m,g}.
